title: MITOCHONDRIAL COMPLEX I DEFICIENCY, NUCLEAR TYPE 7

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC1DN7) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NDUFV2 gene (600532) on chromosome 18p11.

checks.claim: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC1DN7) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NDUFV2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We have identified NDUFV2 mutations in two families with Complex I deficiency, including a novel mutation.
checks.explanation: Compound heterozygous mutations in one family and a homozygous mutation in another. The MC1DN7 label is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The NDUFV2 gene is located on chromosome 18p11.
checks.evidence_quote: Two compound heterozygous mutations were identified in both siblings in NDUFV2, encoding the 24 kDa subunit of Complex I.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to a gene the paper names.

paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 7 is an autosomal recessive disorder with decreased activity of mitochondrial complex I. Bénit et al. (2003) and Cameron et al. (2015) described early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with trunk hypotonia or brain atrophy. Cameron et al. (2015) also described a family with Leigh syndrome and no cardiac involvement.

paragraphs.text: Loeffen et al. (2001) studied patients from 3 families with enzymatic complex I deficiency, cardiomyopathy, and encephalomyopathy. They screened NDUFS2 cDNA by RT-PCR and direct sequencing and found 3 missense mutations that changed conserved amino acids. Loeffen et al. (2001) noted a high rate of consanguinity and autosomal recessive inheritance in their group of patients with complex I deficiency. Together with the absence of common mtDNA mutations, this made a nuclear genetic cause likely.

paragraphs.text: Bénit et al. (2003) studied 3 affected sibs from a consanguineous family with complex I deficiency and early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Using denaturing HPLC and sequencing, they identified a homozygous 4-bp deletion in intron 2 of the NDUFV2 gene (IVS2+5_+8delGTAA). The deletion altered the consensus splice-donor site of exon 2. It led to a 70% decrease in NDUFV2 protein and to complex I deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Cameron et al. (2015) studied 2 sibs with complex I deficiency, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and brain atrophy. They performed whole-exome sequencing on fibroblast DNA from one sib and filtered for novel nonsynonymous changes. This identified compound heterozygous mutations in the NDUFV2 gene. One was a previously reported intronic splice mutation (c.IVS2+1delGTAA), considered disease causing. The other was a novel 1-bp insertion (c.669_670insG) predicted to cause a frameshift (p.Ser224Valfs*3).

paragraphs.text: Pagniez-Mammeri et al. (2009) studied 8 patients with biochemically proven isolated mitochondrial complex I deficiency. They screened 8 nuclear complex I genes (NDUFS1, NDUFS2, NDUFS3, NDUFS4, NDUFS7, NDUFS8, NDUFV1, and NDUFV2) by Surveyor nuclease digestion of 22 cDNA fragments covering the coding sequences. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms and missense mutations were detected in 18.7% of the cDNA fragments, and molecular defects were identified in 3 patients. The authors concluded that Surveyor nuclease screening of cDNAs is a reliable and easy-to-interpret way to genotype nuclear complex I deficiencies and that it reduces the number of sequencing reactions needed. They suggested that the method would make prenatal diagnosis more feasible.
